It is called brahmi in parts of India, a name it shares with Bacopa monnieri. Those are different plants in different families, which is the reason the Latin is on the sheet.

ingredients.h2: One leaf, and two plants called brahmi
ingredients.intro: A one ingredient list is a short section. Here is the plant, where it is eaten as food, the row the label leaves empty, and the shell it goes into.

cards.alt: Centella asiatica leaves, round and scalloped, on their stalks
cards.p: A creeping perennial of damp ground across the tropics and subtropics, in the carrot and parsley family. It puts out runners along the soil and sends up round, scalloped leaves on single stalks. The taste is green and slightly bitter.

cards.alt: The shop floor at 599 Smithdown Road, shelves along the wall
cards.p: In Sri Lanka the raw leaf is shredded into a sambol with coconut and lime. In Vietnam it is blended with water and ice and sold cold on the street. That is worth knowing when you are deciding what a capsule of it is, and it is a fact about kitchens rather than about you.

cards.alt: Two plain capsules on a saucer beside a glass of water, a generated scene
cards.p: The parts above ground are what is normally milled under this name. Our listing says 100 per cent of the plant and does not say which part, so this page does not state one. There is no milligram figure printed either.

cards.alt: Plain capsules and a wooden scoop on a slate board, a generated scene
cards.p: The powder goes into a vegan capsule, with no filler, binder or flow agent named on the listing. The shell material itself is not specified. These capsules are a generated scene rather than a photograph of ours.

ingredients.label: What is on the inside

rows: Makeup
One ingredient. Centella asiatica, milled, in a vegan capsule.
Species

Centella asiatica (L.) Urban, family Apiaceae. Sold in English as gotu kola and as Indian pennywort. It is also called brahmi in parts of India, a name shared with Bacopa monnieri, which is a different plant in a different family.
Part used
Not printed. Leaf and stalk are what is usually milled under this name. The listing does not say.
Fill
No fillers and no bulking agents, as the listing states.
Capsule
Vegan. The shell material is not named on the listing.
Count and strength
Not printed. Neither the number of capsules in the jar nor the milligrams in each is on the listing, so there is no day rate on this page.
Constituents
The listing prints a list of plant constituents with no quantity against any of them. A list with no figure is not a specification, so it is not on this sheet.
Origin
Not printed. No country of harvest and no supplier are named.
Price
£19.99. One size. The variant line reads 100 g without saying whether that is powder, filled capsules or the jar, so it is not a strength figure.
Serving
One or two capsules a day with a meal, and at least 500 ml of water. The listing says spring water.
Storage
Dry, out of direct sun, lid on. It does not need a fridge.
Excipients
None named beyond the capsule shell.
Suitable for
Vegans. Adults.
Not for

Children. The listing carries the longest caution on this shelf and we print it as it stands: do not take it if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, if you have liver issues, a history of skin cancer or an operation coming up, or if you take medication for the liver or for diabetes, or a diuretic. If you have an operation booked, stop well beforehand and tell the team you have been taking it. If you take any other prescribed medication, ask your GP or pharmacist first.
spec.smallprint: Do not exceed the stated dose. Speak to your GP or pharmacist before starting any supplement, particularly if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or take medication. Food supplements should not be used as a substitute for a varied and balanced diet and a healthy lifestyle. Keep out of reach of young children.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: The species is named in Latin and separated from the other plant that shares one of its common names. The serving and the price are printed. The count, the milligrams, the part used and the origin are printed as blanks. The caution is printed at its full length rather than trimmed to fit. What gotu kola does in a person is not something we are permitted to say, so it is not on this page.

reiss.label: From Reiss
reiss.h2: When the caution is longer than the ingredient list
paras: The ingredient list on this jar is one line. The list of people who should not take it runs to five. That is the honest shape of this product and I would rather you saw it on the way in than found it on the way out, so it is printed above at full length in the words the listing uses.

A long caution is not a mark against a plant. It usually means somebody has bothered to write down what is known, which is more than you get from a jar that says nothing at all. Read it, and if a line applies to you, put the jar back on the shelf. That is what the line is for.

The rest of the label is thin: no count, no milligrams, no part named, no country. Gotu kola is eaten as a leaf in Sri Lanka and drunk cold in Vietnam, so this is not an unfamiliar plant anywhere, and there is no good reason for those four rows to stay empty. They are on my list.
reiss.pull: A long caution usually means somebody bothered to write down what is known.
